SMOKE ALARM AND CARBON MONOXIDE DEVICE COMPLIANCE DISCLOSURE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

SMOKE ALARM AND CARBON MONOXIDE DEVICE COMPLIANCE DISCLOSURE
This disclosure concerns the property at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, being transferred from Pat Morgan ("Transferor") to Jordan Lee ("Transferee"). It addresses California's separate statutory requirements for smoke alarms and carbon monoxide devices in residential dwellings, and the transferor's compliance statement obligation tied to this transfer.

SMOKE ALARM REQUIREMENT AND TRANSFEROR'S WRITTEN COMPLIANCE STATEMENT
California law requires that every single-family dwelling and factory-built housing which is sold have an operable smoke alarm. At the time of installation, the alarm must be approved and listed by the State Fire Marshal and installed in accordance with the State Fire Marshal's regulations; unless prohibited by local rules, regulations, or ordinances, a battery-operated smoke alarm that met the smoke-alarm standards in effect at the time of installation satisfies this requirement. Separately, the transferor of real property containing such a single-family dwelling — whether the transfer is by sale, exchange, or real property sales contract — must deliver to the transferee a written statement indicating that the transferor is in compliance with this requirement. This disclosure statement may be included in the deposit receipt for the transaction, an addendum attached to it, or a separate document. The transferor must deliver the statement as soon as practicable before transfer of title in the case of a sale or exchange, or before execution of the contract where the transfer is by a real property sales contract.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "On and after January 1, 1986, every single-family dwelling and factory-built housing, as defined in Section 19971, which is sold shall have an operable smoke alarm. At the time of installation, the alarm shall be approved and listed by the State Fire Marshal and installed in accordance with the State Fire Marshal’s regulations. Unless prohibited by local rules, regulations, or ordinances, a battery-operated smoke alarm that met the standards adopted pursuant to Section 13114 for smoke alarms at the time of installation shall be deemed to satisfy the requirements of this section."
  — Health & Safety Code, smoke alarm installation and standard, Health & Safety Code § 13113.8(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=13113.8)
  "On and after January 1, 1986, the transferor of any real property containing a single-family dwelling, as described in subdivision (a), whether the transfer is made by sale, exchange, or real property sales contract, as defined in Section 2985 of the Civil Code, shall deliver to the transferee a written statement indicating that the transferor is in compliance with this section. The disclosure statement shall be either included in the receipt for deposit in a real estate transaction, an addendum attached thereto, or a separate document."
  — Health & Safety Code, transferor's written compliance statement, Health & Safety Code § 13113.8(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=13113.8)
  "The transferor shall deliver the statement referred to in subdivision (b) as soon as practicable before the transfer of title in the case of a sale or exchange, or prior to execution of the contract where the transfer is by a real property sales contract, as defined in Section 2985."
  — Health & Safety Code, delivery timing of the compliance statement, Health & Safety Code § 13113.8(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=13113.8)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction ties a life-safety device standard to a transfer disclosure obligation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer; smoke alarm and disclosure requirements vary by state. The statute's scope term is 'single-family dwelling,' which the statute itself defines to include a one- or two-unit dwelling but to exclude a manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial coach — a narrower and differently-drawn category than the 'single-family residential property' language used in the Transfer Disclosure Statement statute. The citations below to subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) are all subsections of the same statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 13113.8) and are not independent of one another.

TRANSFERS EXEMPT FROM THE SMOKE ALARM COMPLIANCE STATEMENT
The smoke alarm compliance statement requirement does not apply to: transfers required to be preceded by a public report under Business and Professions Code § 11018.1; transfers pursuant to court order, including probate-court sales, writ-of-execution sales, bankruptcy-trustee transfers, eminent domain, or a decree for specific performance; transfers to a mortgagee by a defaulting mortgagor, to a beneficiary of a deed of trust by a defaulting trustor, or by any foreclosure sale or trustee's sale after default; transfers by a fiduciary in the administration of a decedent's estate, guardianship, conservatorship, or trust; transfers from one co-owner to one or more other co-owners; transfers to a spouse or to a person in the lineal line of consanguinity of a transferor; transfers between spouses resulting from a dissolution or legal-separation decree or an incidental property settlement; transfers by the Controller administering the Unclaimed Property Law; and transfers under the Revenue and Taxation Code provisions governing tax-defaulted property sales.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This section does not apply to any of the following: (1) Transfers which are required to be preceded by the furnishing to a prospective transferee of a copy of a public report pursuant to Section 11018.1 of the Business and Professions Code. (2) Transfers pursuant to court order, including, but not limited to, transfers ordered by a probate court in the administration of an estate, transfers pursuant to a writ of execution, transfers by a trustee in bankruptcy, transfers by eminent domain, or transfers resulting from a decree for specific performance."
  — Health & Safety Code, exemptions (1)-(2), Health & Safety Code § 13113.8(d)(1)-(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=13113.8)
  "(3) Transfers to a mortgagee by a mortgagor in default, transfers to a beneficiary of a deed of trust by a trustor in default, transfers by any foreclosure sale after default, transfers by any foreclosure sale after default in an obligation secured by a mortgage, or transfers by a sale under a power of sale after a default in an obligation secured by a deed of trust or secured by any other instrument containing a power of sale. (4) Transfers by a fiduciary in the course of the administration of a decedent’s estate, guardianship, conservatorship, or trust. (5) Transfers from one coowner to one or more coowners. (6) Transfers made to a spouse, or to a person or persons in the lineal line of consanguinity of one or more of the transferors. (7) Transfers between spouses resulting from a decree of dissolution of a marriage, from a decree of legal separation, or from a property settlement agreement incidental to either of those decrees. (8) Transfers by the Controller in the course of administering the Unclaimed Property Law provided for in Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 1500) of Title 10 of Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (9) Transfers under the provisions of Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 3691) or Chapter 8 (commencing with Section 3771) of Part 6 of Division 1 of the Revenue and Taxation Code."
  — Health & Safety Code, exemptions (3)-(9), Health & Safety Code § 13113.8(d)(3)-(9) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=13113.8)
  Known gap: This exemption list overlaps with, but is not identical to, the exemption list this corpus documents for the general Transfer Disclosure Statement requirement: this statute additionally exempts public-report transfers and Unclaimed Property Law and tax-default sale transfers, categories not listed among the TDS exemptions documented elsewhere in this corpus, and each list should be checked on its own terms rather than assumed to mirror the other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's exemption structure for a device-specific transfer disclosure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 13113.8) and are not independent of one another.

SMOKE ALARM STATEMENT: AGENT LIABILITY AND TRANSFER REMEDY
No liability arises against, and no action may be brought or maintained against, any agent of any party to a transfer of title, including a person or entity acting as escrow, for an error, inaccuracy, or omission relating to the smoke alarm compliance statement a transferor must make — except that this protection does not extend to a real estate licensee who participates in making the disclosure with actual knowledge that it is false. This requirement does not create or imply a duty on a licensee or on any agent of a party to the transfer, including an escrow, to monitor or ensure compliance with the smoke alarm requirement. No transfer of title is invalidated for a failure to comply with the smoke alarm requirement; the exclusive remedy for noncompliance is an award of actual damages not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100), exclusive of court costs and attorney's fees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "No liability shall arise, nor any action be brought or maintained against, any agent of any party to a transfer of title, including any person or entity acting in the capacity of an escrow, for any error, inaccuracy, or omission relating to the disclosure required to be made by a transferor pursuant to this section."
  — Health & Safety Code, agent/escrow non-liability except for known-false disclosure, Health & Safety Code § 13113.8(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=13113.8)
  "this section shall not be deemed to create or imply a duty upon a licensee, as defined in Section 10011 of the Business and Professions Code, or upon any agent of any party to a transfer of title, including any person or entity acting in the capacity of an escrow, to monitor or ensure compliance with this section."
  — Health & Safety Code, no duty to monitor compliance, Health & Safety Code § 13113.8(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=13113.8)
  "No transfer of title shall be invalidated on the basis of a failure to comply with this section, and the exclusive remedy for the failure to comply with this section is an award of actual damages not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100), exclusive of any court costs and attorney’s fees."
  — Health & Safety Code, transfer not invalidated; $100 damages cap, Health & Safety Code § 13113.8(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=13113.8)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction caps the remedy for noncompliance with a device-specific transfer disclosure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, or about what remedies (if any) another jurisdiction's law would allow. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 13113.8) and are not independent of one another.

CARBON MONOXIDE DEVICE INSTALLATION REQUIREMENT
Under the Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Prevention Act of 2010, an owner of a dwelling unit intended for human occupancy must install a carbon monoxide device, approved and listed by the State Fire Marshal, in each existing dwelling unit that has a fossil-fuel-burning heater or appliance, a fireplace, or an attached garage. The installation deadline depended on the type of dwelling: on or before July 1, 2011 for existing single-family dwelling units; on or before January 1, 2013 for other existing dwelling units; and on or before January 1, 2017 for existing hotel and motel dwelling units — deadlines that have all now passed, so the installation requirement applies to all covered existing dwelling units as of the date of this disclosure. As to the number and placement of the devices, the owner must install them consistent with the building standards that apply to new construction for the relevant type of occupancy, or with the manufacturer's instructions, where technically feasible.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An owner of a dwelling unit intended for human occupancy shall install a carbon monoxide device, approved and listed by the State Fire Marshal pursuant to Section 13263, in each existing dwelling unit having a fossil fuel burning heater or appliance, fireplace, or an attached garage, within the earliest applicable time period as follows: (1) For all existing single-family dwelling units intended for human occupancy on or before July 1, 2011. (2) For all existing hotel and motel dwelling units intended for human occupancy on or before January 1, 2017. (3) For all other existing dwelling units intended for human occupancy on or before January 1, 2013."
  — Health & Safety Code, carbon monoxide device installation trigger and deadlines, Health & Safety Code § 17926(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=17926)
  "With respect to the number and placement of carbon monoxide devices, an owner shall install the devices in a manner consistent with building standards applicable to new construction for the relevant type of occupancy or with the manufacturer’s instructions, if it is technically feasible to do so."
  — Health & Safety Code, number/placement standard, Health & Safety Code § 17926(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=17926)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a device-installation requirement tied to dwelling occupancy — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dwelling. Unlike the smoke alarm statute, this statute's installation duty is not framed as sale-triggered; it is framed as an ongoing owner obligation tied to occupancy of a dwelling unit having the listed fuel-burning or garage features, and it does not itself state a duty to deliver a written compliance statement to a transferee at the time of a sale comparable to the smoke alarm statute's separate written-statement requirement. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 17926) and are not independent of one another; a separately numbered section, § 17926.1, imposes a related but distinct carbon-monoxide-device maintenance duty on an owner or owner's agent who rents or leases a dwelling unit to a tenant, which is not a transfer-of-title disclosure duty and is not relied on here.

CARBON MONOXIDE DEVICE: VIOLATION PENALTY AND TRANSFER REMEDY
A violation of the carbon monoxide device installation requirement is an infraction punishable by a maximum fine of two hundred dollars ($200) per offense, but a property owner must first receive a 30-day notice to correct, and the fine may be assessed only if the owner fails to correct within that period. Separately, no transfer of title is invalidated for a failure to comply with the carbon monoxide device requirement; the exclusive remedy for noncompliance is an award of actual damages not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100), exclusive of court costs and attorney's fees, and this limit does not affect any other duties, rights, or remedies otherwise available at law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "a violation of this section is an infraction punishable by a maximum fine of two hundred dollars ($200) for each offense. (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a property owner shall receive a 30-day notice to correct. If an owner receiving notice fails to correct within that time period, the owner may be assessed the fine pursuant to paragraph (2)."
  — Health & Safety Code, infraction fine and 30-day cure notice, Health & Safety Code § 17926(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=17926)
  "No transfer of title shall be invalidated on the basis of a failure to comply with this section, and the exclusive remedy for the failure to comply with this section is an award of actual damages not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100), exclusive of any court costs and attorney’s fees. This subdivision is not intended to affect any duties, rights, or remedies otherwise available at law."
  — Health & Safety Code, transfer not invalidated; $100 damages cap, Health & Safety Code § 17926(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=17926)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures both a code-enforcement penalty and a separate, capped transfer-related remedy for the same device requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dwelling or transfer. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 17926) and are not independent of one another; they are also not independent of the installation-requirement citations in the preceding clause, which cite different subsections of this same section.

TRANSFEROR'S STATEMENT AND SIGNATURES
Transferor's statement: The undersigned transferor states that the smoke alarm(s) installed at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield are, to the transferor's knowledge, in compliance with the smoke alarm requirements described above.

Signed:

☐ _________________________ Pat Morgan (Transferor)   Date: _______________

☐ _________________________ Jordan Lee (Transferee)   Date: _______________
